stem: A 4-year-old boy has had recurrent skin abscesses and now has a lung abscess. A dihydrorhodamine test shows no oxidative burst. The abscess grows a catalase-positive, oxidase-negative gram-negative rod that forms red colonies at room temperature.
oneliner: 4M + recurrent abscesses + lung abscess + absent DHR burst + catalase-positive, oxidase-negative GNR, red colonies at room temperature → which organism?
ask: Which organism most likely grew from the abscess?

whyNot.A: Catalase-positive CGD organism, but **gram-positive cocci** with golden colonies
whyNot.B: Catalase-positive CGD lung pathogen, but **oxidase-positive** and **not red**
whyNot.C: Catalase-positive CGD lung pathogen, but **gram-positive branching rods**, weakly acid-fast

why: Without **NADPH oxidase**, phagocytes make no respiratory burst, so **catalase-positive** organisms that destroy their own peroxide survive. All five options are catalase-positive CGD pathogens; only **Serratia** is an **oxidase-negative gram-negative rod** with **red pigment** (prodigiosin).

idea.rule: CGD patients fall to catalase-positive organisms: Staph aureus, Serratia, Burkholderia cepacia, Nocardia, Aspergillus.
also: Catalase-negative streptococci are killed using their own peroxide
Burkholderia cepacia is a major pulmonary pathogen in CGD
Nocardia and Aspergillus also affect the lungs

bug.name: Serratia marcescens
bug.lab: Red pigment (prodigiosin) at room temperature; slow lactose fermenter
bug.virulence: Catalase breaks down peroxide; LPS endotoxin
bug.spread: Hospital environment, catheters, contaminated water and equipment
bug.causes: Hospital UTI, pneumonia and bacteremia; serious infections in CGD
